title: Operation Market Garden
wiki_lead:
Operation Market Garden was an Allied military operation during the Second World War, fought in the German-occupied Netherlands from 17 to 25 September 1944. Its objective was to create a salient spanning 62 miles (100 km) into German territory with a bridgehead over the Nederrijn (Lower Rhine River), creating an Allied invasion route into northern Germany. This was to be achieved by two sub-operations: seizing nine bridges with combined American, British and Polish airborne forces ("Market") followed by British land forces swiftly following over the bridges ("Garden").
The airborne operation was undertaken by the First Allied Airborne Army with the land operation by the British Second Army, with XXX Corps moving up the centre supported by VIII and XII Corps on their flanks. The airborne soldiers, consisting of paratroops and  glider-borne troops numbering around 35,000–40,000, were dropped at sites where they could capture key bridges and hold the terrain until the land forces arrived. The land forces consisted of ten armoured and motorised brigades with approximately 800 tanks and 50,000 soldiers. The land forces advanced from the south along a single road partly surrounded by flood plain on both sides. The plan anticipated that they would cover the 62 miles (100 km) from their start at the Belgian–Dutch border to the Arnhem bridge across the Lower Rhine in 48 hours. About 100,000 German soldiers were in the vicinity to oppose the allied offensive. It was the largest airborne operation of the war up to that point.
The operation succeeded in capturing the Dutch cities of Eindhoven and Nijmegen along with many towns, and a few V-2 rocket launching sites. It failed in its most important objective: securing the bridge over the Rhine at Arnhem. The British 1st Airborne Division was unable to secure the bridge and was withdrawn from the north side of the Rhine after suffering 8,000 dead, missing, and captured out of a complement of 10,000 men. When the retreat order came, there were not enough boats to get everyone back across the river. The Germans subsequently rounded up most of those left behind, but some of the British and Polish paratroopers managed to avoid capture by the Germans and were sheltered by the Dutch underground until they could be rescued in Operation Pegasus on 22 October 1944. Historians have been critical of the planning and execution of Operation Market Garden. Antony Beevor said that Market Garden "was a bad plan right from the start and right from the top".
The Germans counterattacked the Nijmegen salient but failed to retake any of the Allied gains. Arnhem was finally captured by the Allies in April 1945, towards the end of the war.

grok_lead: Operation Market Garden was a major Allied military operation during World War II, conducted from 17 to 25 September 1944 in the German-occupied Netherlands, which combined airborne assaults to seize key bridges with a ground advance to create a corridor into Germany and potentially end the war by Christmas. The operation, code-named "Market" for the airborne phase and "Garden" for the ground element, was proposed by British Field Marshal Bernard Montgomery and involved the largest airborne assault in history, with approximately 35,000 paratroopers and glider troops from the First Allied Airborne Army, including the U.S. 101st and 82nd Airborne Divisions, the British 1st Airborne Division, and the Polish 1st Parachute Brigade. The primary objective was to capture a series of bridges over the Maas ( Meuse), Waal, and Lower Rhine rivers at locations including Eindhoven, Nijmegen, Grave, and Arnhem, allowing the British XXX Corpsâled by the Guards Armoured Division âto advance rapidly toward the Ruhr industrial region in western Germany. Launched on 17 September with massive daylight parachute drops behind enemy lines, the operation achieved initial successes, such as the capture of the Eindhoven bridge and, after fierce fighting, the Nijmegen bridges, but encountered severe delays due to unexpectedly strong German resistance from SS Panzer divisions and logistical challenges like narrow roads and poor weather. At Arnhem, the northernmost objective, British airborne forces were isolated and overwhelmed after only one battalion reached the vital Rhine bridge, leading to a desperate defense and eventual withdrawal. Despite securing a salient up to Nijmegen and liberating parts of the Netherlands, Operation Market Garden ultimately failed to cross the Rhine, resulting in heavy Allied casualtiesâestimated at over 15,000, including around 1,500 killed and more than 6,000 capturedâand delaying further advances into Germany by several months. The operation highlighted the risks of ambitious airborne tactics against fortified positions and contributed to postwar debates on Allied strategy, though it demonstrated the bravery of the troops involved and paved the way for subsequent offensives like Operation Veritable in 1945.
